introduction-why-rust-for-ops.core: Rust gives C-level speed and memory safety with no garbage collector. That suits infrastructure where latency, footprint and security bugs really matter: proxies, agents, runtimes.

first_principles.problem: Ops tooling went Bash → Python → Go, but some components (data planes, eBPF agents, edge proxies) need tighter control than Go's GC allows.
truths: Most security vulnerabilities in C/C++ are memory bugs.
derivation: Get **safety at compile time** rather than at runtime.
**Zero-cost abstractions** give high-level code low-level speed.
Use it where those properties pay off.

analogy.title: A race car with an automatic safety inspector
analogy.story: It's as fast as an unsafe car, but an inspector refuses to let you drive off with loose bolts.
analogy.breaks: The inspector is strict, so the learning curve is steep and compiling is slower.

example.title: A sidecar proxy at 100k req/s
flow: Go: GC pauses add p99 spikes
Choose Rust for the hot data path

steps.label: Examples
steps.detail: Linkerd2-proxy, Firecracker and parts of AWS's infrastructure use Rust.

example.outcome: Rust is used where performance and safety are critical.

check.q: What gap does Rust fill compared with Go?
check.a: Memory safety with no garbage collector, giving predictable latency and a small footprint.

the-core-promise-memory-safety-without-g.core: Manual memory management (C) is fast but unsafe, and garbage collection is safe but adds pauses. Rust decides at compile time when each value is freed, giving safety with no runtime cost.

first_principles.problem: Programs must free memory they no longer need. Getting it wrong causes crashes and security holes; automating it at runtime costs performance.
truths: Every allocation must be freed exactly once.
A GC runs at runtime and pauses work.
derivation: C: the programmer frees, **fast but error-prone**.
Java/Go: the GC frees, **safe but with pauses**.
Rust: the **compiler proves** where to free, so it's **safe and fast**.

analogy.title: Three ways to tidy a library
analogy.story: Readers reshelve books themselves (they forget), a janitor sweeps periodically (closes the library while sweeping), or every book has a return date enforced at checkout.
analogy.breaks: Rust also has escape hatches (`unsafe`, Rc), and safety is only guaranteed outside them.

example.title: Use-after-free
example.scenario: C compiles it; Rust rejects it.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: A whole class of bugs never reaches production.

example.outcome: you get memory safety with no runtime overhead.

check.q: When does Rust decide to free memory?
check.a: At compile time, when the owner goes out of scope.

the-borrow-checker-the-compilers-bouncer.core: Each value has exactly one owner, and it's dropped when the owner goes out of scope. You can lend it as many read-only borrows OR exactly one mutable borrow. The borrow checker enforces this at compile time.

first_principles.problem: Concurrent readers and writers on shared data cause data races and dangling pointers.
truths: Reading while someone writes is unsafe.
References must not outlive their data.
derivation: **Lifetimes**: a borrow can't outlive the owner.

analogy.title: A nightclub bouncer and a library book
analogy.story: Many people can read a reference copy together, but only one person at a time can check out the copy to write in it.
analogy.breaks: The rules sometimes reject valid programs, so you restructure or use Rc or RefCell.

example.title: Mutating while iterating

steps.label: Insight
steps.detail: In other languages this is a runtime bug; here it's a compile error.

code.text:
let mut v = vec![1, 2];
for x in &v { v.push(*x); }  // error: cannot borrow v mutably while borrowed

example.outcome: data races are impossible in safe code.

check.q: Can you hold a &mut and a & to the same value at once?
check.a: No. Either many shared borrows or one mutable borrow.

asyncawait-and-tokio-concurrency-for-ops.core: Async Rust lets one thread juggle thousands of I/O waits. `async fn` returns a future, `.await` yields while waiting, and the Tokio runtime schedules the futures across threads.

first_principles.problem: Infra tools mostly wait on the network, and a thread per connection wastes memory at scale.
truths: Rust needs a runtime library to drive futures.
derivation: **Tokio** provides the executor, timers and networking.

analogy.title: A waiter serving many tables
analogy.story: The waiter takes an order and moves on while the kitchen cooks, rather than standing at one table until its food arrives.
analogy.breaks: CPU-heavy work blocks the waiter, so move it to spawn_blocking.

example.title: Concurrent health checks

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Hundreds of checks run on a few threads.

example.outcome: high-concurrency I/O with a tiny footprint.

check.q: Why shouldn't you call blocking code inside async tasks?
check.a: It stalls the runtime thread, starving every other task scheduled on it.

compilation-targets-the-power-of-static-.core: Compiling for the `x86_64-unknown-linux-musl` target links everything, libc included, into one static binary that runs on any Linux, whatever its glibc version.

first_principles.problem: A binary built on a new distro fails on an older server with 'GLIBC_2.34 not found'.
truths: Dynamic linking depends on the host's libraries.

analogy.title: Packing your own power adapter
analogy.story: Wherever you travel, your device works, because you aren't relying on the hotel's sockets.
analogy.breaks: musl's allocator can be slower, and some crates need system C libraries.

example.title: An agent for a mixed fleet

steps.label: Result
steps.detail: The same binary runs on every host.

code.text:
cargo build --release --target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl
ldd target/x86_64-unknown-linux-musl/release/agent  # not a dynamic executable

check.q: Why does a glibc-linked binary fail on old servers?
check.a: It requires a newer glibc version than the server has installed.

rust-vs-go-for-infrastructure.core: Go optimises for team speed and simplicity, Rust for runtime performance and correctness. Pick Go for most control-plane tools and Rust for hot data paths and safety-critical low-level work.

first_principles.problem: Teams argue about languages by taste rather than by the properties a component needs.
truths: Developer time and machine time both cost money.
derivation: **Go**: fast to learn, great ecosystem, GC is fine for most cases.
**Rust**: no GC, maximum control, steeper learning curve.
Ask about **latency, footprint, team skills and ecosystem**.
Mixing is fine: a Go control plane with a Rust data plane.

analogy.title: A minivan vs. a sports car
analogy.story: The minivan carries the whole team easily; the sports car wins on the racetrack but needs a trained driver.
analogy.breaks: Both are excellent. The 'wrong' choice is usually fine, while fighting your ecosystem isn't.

example.title: Building a service mesh
example.outcome: each component gets the language that suits it.

check.q: When is Rust the better choice than Go?
check.a: For latency-critical, memory-constrained or safety-critical components such as data-plane proxies.

the-ecosystem-cargo-and-key-crates-for-o.core: Cargo is Rust's single build tool and package manager. Ops staples include tokio (async), reqwest (HTTP), serde (serialisation), clap (CLI parsing), tracing (logs) and anyhow/thiserror (errors).

first_principles.problem: C and C++ build ecosystems are fragmented and painful, while Rust standardises everything on one tool.
truths: Mature crates exist for common ops needs.

analogy.title: An all-in-one kitchen appliance
analogy.story: One machine handles shopping (deps), cooking (build), tasting (test) and plating (release).
analogy.breaks: Dependency trees can get large, so audit them with cargo-audit or cargo-deny.

check.a: It pins exact dependency versions for reproducible builds.
